newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish court sentences two for U.S. report.
newsitem.headline: Turkish court sentences two for U.S. report.

text.p: An Istanbul court sentenced two Turks on Friday for insulting Turkey's army by translating a rights report containing an allegedly offensive quote by a diplomat from the United States, Ankara's longstanding ally.
Ertugrul Kurkcu, who translated the report by the U.S.-based Human Rights Watch, was given a 10-month suspended sentence and publisher Aysenur Zarakolu was fined 1.5 million lira ($12).

"We knew the verdict would be 'guilty' as the trial is political," Kurkcu told reporters. "The striking part is that we are condemned not for our own words but those of a U.S. embassy official who has been quoted in the report."

The 1995 report, "Weapons transfers and violations of the laws of war in Turkey", criticises Ankara's handling of a 12-year-old Kurdish rebel conflict in the southeast and quotes an unnamed senior official at the U.S. embassy in Turkey as describing crack Turkish policemen as "brutal thugs".
Rights activists saw the court's decision not to order jail time as something of a compromise.

They said it proved the court acted under political pressure, bearing in mind the need to show the government as being tough at home while ensuring it avoided condemnation by the West, already critical of Turkey's shaky rights record.

"I think in a sense it underscores the weakness of the original charges and shows an attempt by the court to find a middle way out," Vincent McGee, vice chairman of the Human Rights Watch Arms Project advisory committee, told Reuters.
"I would say they feel that to impose a real fine would be too much but they don't feel free to exonerate the defendants," McGee said.

The fines prescribed under the Turkish penal code are generally very low as the code has not been revised for years and the value of the sums have been diminished by inflation running around 80 percent annually.

In a separate case in Ankara, a state security court released one Kurdish politician but kept 13 others jailed in a hearing nine months into the trial on charges of alleged links with separatist Kurds. The trial will continue at a later date.

Forty-one members of the People's Democratic Party (HADEP), including party leader Murat Bozlak, were arrested after a party congress last June in which a Turkish flag was torn down and replaced with banners linked to the Kurdish rebels.
The European Parliament has blocked millions of dollars of aid to Ankara, partly as a result of Turkey's rights problems.

A U.N. human rights report on Thursday accused Turkey of a long list of abuses, including imprisonment of writers, police torture of journalists, use of force against protesters and routine seizure of newspapers.

The Foreign Ministry announced this week that Ankara was going to act to improve human rights, focusing on preventing torture in police custody, strengthening efforts to find missing people and increasing freedom of expression.
Parliament passed a law last week which reduces the maximum detention period for collective crimes in Turkey's nine emergency rule provinces to one week from 30 days previously.
